actions.body: The consensus of an epistemic community is frequently cited as a baseline for truth, yet deference models suggest that rational agents must weigh the reliability of that consensus against their own private information. When information sources are correlated or the consensus generation mechanism is opaque, total deference can lead to systemic error. Our analysis of recent literature suggests that epistemic deference is contingent upon the transparency of the consensus-forming process and the independence of evidence channels. Without these, consensus may propagate existing biases rather than refining accuracy, necessitating a robust framework for when an agent should prioritize internal validation over external agreement.
actions.lede: When agents aggregate information, consensus models often assume rational deference; however, empirical and theoretical scrutiny reveals structural conditions where independent judgment remains necessary for accuracy.
actions.reason: Synthesizing the current understanding of consensus reliability and epistemic deference based on available evidence, fulfilling the project requirements for active research documentation.
actions.title: Revisiting Deference Models in Consensus

What are the propositional attitude(s) involved in collective epistemic agency? There are two opposing camps on this question: the ascribers have defended an extended notion of belief, while the rejectionists have claimed that groups form goal-sensitive acceptances. Addressing this question, however, requires providing responses to four preliminary queries. (1) Are group attitudes reducible to the participants’ attitudes? (2) Is epistemic evaluation sensitive to instrumental considerations? (3) Does accepting that p entail believing that p? (4) Is there a unity of epistemic rationality across levels? Both “believing” and “accepting as true”, as applied to plural subjects, fail to provide satisfactory answers to these four queries. An alternative analysis for epistemic group attitude called “accepting under consensus” is proposed. This attitude is shown to reflect actual group agency, and to offer consistent and independently justified answers to the queries. On this analysis, an individualist epistemology cannot simply be transferred to collective agents.

actions.body: Existing evidence on epistemic deference suggests that consensus models are powerful but bounded. We define independent judgment as a function of evidence reliability and the independence of the agent's observation process. When consensus relies on shared, potentially flawed initial assumptions, independent judgment—if based on distinct, verified data—is epistemically superior. The synthesis indicates that deference is rational only when the epistemic authority of the consensus source is demonstrably higher and independent of the agent's own error-prone processes. We avoid blind reliance by requiring explicit criteria for when to trust consensus over local evidence.
actions.lede: When should an intelligent agent maintain independent judgment in the face of consensus?
